result.markdown: # Tutorial 1: Simple regression, diagnostics, and model usefulness {#i-ep01} ::: {.outcomes} By the end of Tutorial 1, you can - fit and interpret a simple regression in R, with units - calculate fitted values and residuals by hand - find problems with the assumptions from residual plots, standardised residuals, and Cook's distance - interpret the coefficient table, $R^2$, and the F-test together - write a short interpretation of a model that is ready for the exam format. ::: Tutorials are **exam preparation sessions**. Every task below follows the format of the final exam, which is taken in TestVision with R available. You first try each task in pairs. You may use AI for this, following Attempt, Ask, Verify, Explain. Then the solution is discussed together. The tasks follow the order of the course. Tasks 1 and 2 use Lecture 1, Task 3 uses Lecture 2, and Tasks 4 and 5 use Lecture 3. Task 6 applies all steps to a new question that matters to founders. ::: {.course-phase .phase-before} ## Before class Complete the after-class practice from Lectures 1 and 2. Lecture 3 is on the day before this tutorial: read its lecture material, and do its practice after the tutorial. Keep the Lectures 1--3 sections of the [QM Intermediate Code Sheet](#intermediate-code-sheet) open while working. If the notation slows you down, review [Mathematics Refresher: lines, squares, and standardisation](../resources/math-refresher.html). Write from memory: 1. the simple linear regression model 2. the fitted line 3. the residual 4. the formula for $R^2$ 5. the null hypothesis of the overall model F-test. ::: {.callout-note collapse="true"} ## Check your preparation 1. $Y_i=\beta_0+\beta_1X_i+\varepsilon_i$. 2. $\widehat Y_i=\hat\beta_0+\hat\beta_1X_i$. 3. $e_i=Y_i-\widehat Y_i$. 4. $R^2=1-\text{SSE}/\text{SST}=\text{SSR}/\text{SST}$. 5. $H_0:\beta_1=0$ in simple regression (all slopes zero in general). ::: ::: ::: {.course-phase .phase-in-class} ## In the tutorial Attempt each task in R before opening the answer. A complete written answer names the sample, shows the calculation, reports values with units, interprets them in context, and states one important limit of the model or of the data. All tasks use the Shark Tank teaching file and the valuations of Lectures 1 to 3, in **millions of dollars**: the valuation agreed on air (`agreed_m`) and the valuation claimed by the founder (`claimed_m`). Build the data once, in the same way as in Lectures 1--3: ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} sharks <- read.csv("data/shark_tank_teaching.csv", stringsAsFactors = FALSE) vals <- subset(sharks, deal_on_show == 1 & deal_equity_pct > 0) vals$claimed_m <- vals$requested_valuation_usd / 1e6 vals$agreed_m <- vals$deal_valuation_usd / 1e6 nrow(vals) # deals for a share of the company ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` [1] 874 ``` ::: ::: ### Task 1: Fit and interpret (Lecture 1) Fit `agreed_m ~ claimed_m` among the deals for a share of the company. Report the sample, the fitted equation, the interpretation of the slope with units, and the limit of the intercept. ::: {.callout-note collapse="true"} ## Check your answer ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} val_model <- lm(agreed_m ~ claimed_m, data = vals) coef(val_model) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` (Intercept) claimed_m -0.06798986 0.64874084 ``` ::: ::: Among the 874 deals for a share of the company, the fitted equation is $\widehat y = -0.068 + 0.649x$, with both valuations in \$ millions. A claimed valuation that is \$1 million higher is associated with an agreed valuation about \$0.65 million higher. A claimed valuation of zero is outside the observed range, so the intercept (about $-\$68{,}000$) has no useful business meaning of its own. ::: ### Task 2: Fitted value and residual (Lecture 1) A founder claimed a valuation of \$5 million and the deal closed at a valuation of \$2.5 million. 1. Calculate its fitted value. 2. Calculate its residual. 3. Interpret the sign of the residual. ::: {.callout-note collapse="true"} ## Check your answer With $x=5$ (in \$ millions), $\widehat y = -0.068 + 0.649 \times 5 \approx 3.18$, or about \$3.18 million. The observed $y = 2.5$, so $e = 2.5 - 3.18 = -0.68$, about $-\$680{,}000$. The negative sign means this deal closed below the model's fitted conditional mean for a claimed valuation of \$5 million. ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} val_model <- lm(agreed_m ~ claimed_m, data = vals) unname(2.5 - predict(val_model, newdata = data.frame(claimed_m = 5))) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` [1] -0.6757143 ``` ::: ::: ::: ### Task 3: Diagnostics and influence (Lecture 2) Produce the residual-versus-fitted plot and the normal Q--Q plot for the Task 1 model. 1. Name two problems with the assumptions that you can see in the plots. 2. Count the standardised residuals beyond $\pm 3$ and the observations with a Cook's distance above $4/n$. 3. State the three-step rule for handling a flagged observation. 4. Name one assumption these plots cannot assess and what would assess it. ::: {.callout-note collapse="true"} ## Check your answer ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} val_model <- lm(agreed_m ~ claimed_m, data = vals) old_par <- par(no.readonly = TRUE) par(mfrow = c(1, 2), mar = c(4.5, 4.4, 1.3, 0.7), las = 1) plot(fitted(val_model), residuals(val_model), pch = 16, col = grDevices::adjustcolor("#0072B2", alpha.f = 0.35), bty = "n", xlab = "Fitted agreed valuation ($ millions)", ylab = "Residual ($ millions)") abline(h = 0, lty = 2, lwd = 2, col = "#D55E00") qqnorm(rstandard(val_model), pch = 16, col = grDevices::adjustcolor("#009E73", alpha.f = 0.40), bty = "n", main = "", xlab = "Normal theoretical quantile", ylab = "Standardised residual") qqline(rstandard(val_model), col = "#D55E00", lwd = 2) ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](t01-exam-prep_files/figure-html/iep01-task3-1.png){width=672} ::: ```{.r .cell-code} par(old_par) c(big_rstandard = sum(abs(rstandard(val_model)) > 3), cooks_flagged = sum(cooks.distance(val_model) > 4 / nrow(vals))) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` big_rstandard cooks_flagged 25 64 ``` ::: ::: The spread of the residuals widens with the fitted value. This fan challenges constant conditional variance. The Q--Q plot leaves the line at both ends, with several extreme residuals on both sides. This challenges normality and points to possibly influential deals. Twenty-five standardised residuals lie beyond $\pm3$, and 64 observations have a Cook's distance above $4/n$. The rule for flagged observations: investigate, report, never silently delete. The plots cannot assess independence or the absence of confounding. Those need knowledge of how the data were collected, for example whether the same sharks or founders appear in several rows. ::: ### Task 4: Coefficient inference (Lecture 3) Use `summary()` and `confint()` on the Task 1 model. 1. Test $H_0:\beta_1=0$ against the two-sided alternative. 2. Report the 95% confidence interval for $\beta_1$, and verify it by hand from the estimate and the standard error. 3. Would robust standard errors ([Lecture 3](i03-inference-fit-ftest.qmd#i03-robust)) fix both problems from Task 3? ::: {.callout-note collapse="true"} ## Check your answer ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} val_model <- lm(agreed_m ~ claimed_m, data = vals) summary(val_model)$coefficients ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` Estimate Std. Error t value Pr(>|t|) (Intercept) -0.06798986 0.06847892 -0.9928582 3.210545e-01 claimed_m 0.64874084 0.01106883 58.6096854 1.099793e-304 ``` ::: ```{.r .cell-code} confint(val_model) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` 2.5 % 97.5 % (Intercept) -0.2023926 0.06641292 claimed_m 0.6270162 0.67046551 ``` ::: ::: The slope is $0.649$ with standard error $0.0111$, so $t \approx 58.6$ on $872$ degrees of freedom and the p-value is far below 0.001: reject a zero slope. By hand, with one more digit to avoid rounding error, $0.6487 \pm 1.96 \times 0.01107 = 0.6487 \pm 0.0217 = (0.627,\; 0.670)$. This matches `confint()`, in \$ million agreed per \$ million claimed. Robust standard errors address the unequal variance only. They do not help with influential observations, with the selection of pitches that ended in a deal, or with a relationship that is not linear. ::: ### Task 5: R² and F (Lecture 3) 1. Calculate SST, SSE, SSR, and $R^2$ manually. 2. Verify them against `summary()`. 3. Verify $F = t^2$. 4. Write one concluding sentence that does not overclaim. ::: {.callout-note collapse="true"} ## Check your answer ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} val_model <- lm(agreed_m ~ claimed_m, data = vals) y <- vals$agreed_m yhat <- fitted(val_model) SST <- sum((y - mean(y))^2) SSE <- sum((y - yhat)^2) SSR <- sum((yhat - mean(y))^2) c(R2_manual = 1 - SSE / SST, R2_summary = summary(val_model)$r.squared, F_summary = unname(summary(val_model)$fstatistic["value"]), t_squared = summary(val_model)$coefficients["claimed_m", "t value"]^2) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` R2_manual R2_summary F_summary t_squared 0.7975434 0.7975434 3435.0952236 3435.0952236 ``` ::: ::: The sums (in squared \$ millions) satisfy $\text{SST}=\text{SSR}+\text{SSE}$, and $R^2 \approx 0.798$. The overall F statistic is about 3435, equal to the squared slope t statistic, as it must be in simple regression. A sentence that does not overclaim: among these deals, the claimed valuation explains about 80% of the variation in the agreed valuations, but this is an association in a selected set of deals, shaped partly by a few influential ones, and not the effect of changing a claim. ::: ### Task 6: A new question: how much more equity do the sharks take? Lecture 1 showed that the sharks usually pay the amount asked and take a larger share of the company. Model that directly. Use all 882 deals and regress the equity agreed in the deal on the equity the founder first offered, both in percent of the company: ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} all_deals <- subset(sharks, deal_on_show == 1) equity_model <- lm(deal_equity_pct ~ equity_offered_pct, data = all_deals) nrow(all_deals) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` [1] 882 ``` ::: ```{.r .cell-code} summary(equity_model)$coefficients ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` Estimate Std. Error t value Pr(>|t|) (Intercept) 8.315024 0.7477311 11.12034 5.684681e-27 equity_offered_pct 1.207341 0.0511365 23.61017 7.368475e-96 ``` ::: ```{.r .cell-code} confint(equity_model) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` 2.5 % 97.5 % (Intercept) 6.847480 9.782569 equity_offered_pct 1.106978 1.307705 ``` ::: ```{.r .cell-code} summary(equity_model)$r.squared ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` [1] 0.3878006 ``` ::: ::: 1. Interpret the slope and the intercept with units. 2. A founder offers 10% of the company. Which agreed share does the model fit? 3. Compare the $R^2$ with the valuation model. What does the difference tell a founder? 4. Advise the founder in two sentences. ::: {.callout-note collapse="true"} ## Check your answer The slope is about 1.21 percentage points of agreed equity per percentage point offered, with a 95% interval of about 1.11 to 1.31. The intercept is about 8.3 percentage points. A founder who offers 10% is fitted to give up $8.3 + 1.21\times10\approx20.4$% of the company, about twice the offer. $R^2$ is about 0.39, against 0.80 for the valuations. The offered share says much less about the agreed share than the claimed valuation says about the agreed valuation, so single deals scatter widely around the line. Advice: expect to give up roughly twice the share you offer, and decide before the pitch how far you are willing to go. These are deals that happened on a television show. They describe what founders who closed a deal gave up, not what would happen to you if you offered a different share. ::: ::: ::: {.course-phase .phase-after} ## After class ### Timed individual practice: 20 minutes Fit `equity_offered_pct ~ season` using all 1,441 records. 1. Make and read the scatterplot with the fitted line. 2. Report the fitted equation and units. 3. Report the standard error of the slope, its t value, its p-value, and its 95% interval. 4. Report $R^2$ and the overall F-test. 5. Inspect the residual plots and write a conclusion of about 120 words. ::: {.callout-note collapse="true"} ## Check a model answer ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} sharks <- read.csv("data/shark_tank_teaching.csv", stringsAsFactors = FALSE) season_model <- lm(equity_offered_pct ~ season, data = sharks) summary(season_model)$coefficients ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` Estimate Std. Error t value Pr(>|t|) (Intercept) 20.4565874 0.46442667 44.04697 4.922706e-269 season -0.8241241 0.04752298 -17.34159 2.514546e-61 ``` ::: ```{.r .cell-code} confint(season_model) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` 2.5 % 97.5 % (Intercept) 19.5455616 21.3676132 season -0.9173458 -0.7309023 ``` ::: ```{.r .cell-code} c(r_squared = summary(season_model)$r.squared, F = unname(summary(season_model)$fstatistic["value"])) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` r_squared F 0.1728605 300.7308055 ``` ::: ::: The fitted equation is $\widehat{equity}=20.457-0.824\,season$: one later season is associated with about 0.824 percentage points less initial equity offered on average. The standard error is about 0.048, $t\approx-17.3$, and the p-value is below 0.001. The 95% interval $(-0.917,\,-0.731)$ excludes zero. $R^2\approx0.173$, so the season explains about 17.3% of the variation in the equity offered, and the overall F-test ($F\approx300.7=t^2$) reaches the same conclusion as the slope test. The residual plot shows sixteen vertical stripes (the season takes whole numbers only) with broadly similar spread. The Q--Q plot bends upwards at the right end because of some very high offers. This is a trend over time among recorded pitches, not a causal effect of a later season. ::: ### Check your understanding Complete from memory: 1. A residual is ... 2. The slope's standard error estimates ... 3. A fan in the residual plot challenges ... 4. $R^2$ is the proportion of ... 5. In simple regression, the overall F statistic equals ... ::: {.callout-note collapse="true"} ## Check your answers 1. The observed outcome minus the fitted value, $e_i=Y_i-\widehat Y_i$. 2. How much the estimated slope would vary from sample to sample, under the model assumptions. 3. Constant conditional variance (homoskedasticity), and with it the usual standard errors. 4. The variation of the outcome in the sample that the fitted values explain, $\text{SSR}/\text{SST}$. 5. The squared slope t statistic, $F=t^2$. ::: ### Make it yours (5 minutes) :::: {.utility-prompt} Utility: two sentences Think of your EiA3 venture, or any business you know well. Imagine the one simple regression you would show an investor (revenue on customers, orders on ad spend), and write two sentences. First name the number from this tutorial you would put in the headline, slope, interval, or $R^2$, and say why. Then name the limit from Task 3 or Task 5 that you would state openly next to it. There is no wrong answer. ::: {.callout-note collapse="true"} ## See an example, then write your own Take a student-run campus meal-prep box venture. "Headline: the slope with its 95% interval. Each extra €100 of ads is associated with roughly 12 to 19 more orders. An investor asks what money buys, and the interval shows how uncertain the number is. Limit: the fan in my residual plot means that busy weeks vary more, so the interval rests on an assumption that my own residual plot puts in doubt." ::: You can discuss this task, and any other task in this tutorial, with **Tilly**, the course AI assistant: paste your two sentences and ask it to play the sceptical investor. :::: [Continue to Lecture 4: Multiple regression and what controls do](i04-multiple-regression.qmd). :::
